passage: The community centre's back room smelled of chalk dust and someone's frying pakoras. Every Saturday, fifteen-year-old Jagdish sat on a plastic stool with three Class 4 kids and a box of bottle caps. "Seven caps, take away three. How many?" Little Preeti counted on her fingers, then shouted, "Four!" and looked at him as if he had invented numbers. Jagdish grinned. At school that week he had come nineteenth in the maths test, and nobody had looked at him at all. Here the kids waited at the door for him, and Preeti's mother had told him, "She talks about Jagdish bhaiya all week." Walking home, he realised he hadn't checked his phone once in two hours.

qa.q: What did Jagdish use to teach subtraction?
qa.a: A box of bottle caps.

qa.q: What does Jagdish not checking his phone for two hours suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt happy and needed at the centre, in a way he didn't feel at school after coming nineteenth.

qa.q: What choice could help Jagdish keep this sense of worth?
qa.a: He could keep the Saturday sessions going even in exam weeks and value them as much as his test rank.

qa.q: How does Preeti see Jagdish?
qa.a: To her he is someone amazing, as if he had invented numbers; she talks about Jagdish bhaiya all week.

grounding: A teenager who tutors younger children feels needed and valued in a way his test rank never gave him.

passage:
Hi Naveen bhai,
Remember the empty plot behind our building where we used to play? It had turned into a dump. Plastic, broken chairs, a dead scooter. Last month I got fed up and stuck a note in the lift: Sunday 7 am, bring gloves.
I thought five people would come. Twenty-two came, including old Mr D'Souza with his walking stick, handing out bags. We filled forty sacks. The municipal van took them on Monday after Ammi and I called three times.
Here's the weird part. My marks this term are average, and nobody at school notices me. But on Sunday people kept asking, "Farhan, where should this go?" as if I knew. I felt needed. That feeling beats any rank.
We're painting the wall next month. Wish you were here.
Your cousin brother,
Farhan

qa.q: How many people came to the cleanup?
qa.a: Twenty-two came.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when people kept asking where things should go?
qa.a: Farhan felt needed and trusted, a feeling that beats any rank.

qa.q: What small first step turned Farhan's frustration into action?
qa.a: A note in the lift with a time and a simple ask, bring gloves, which made it easy for neighbours to join.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Souza have felt joining the cleanup?
qa.a: He may have felt useful and part of the neighbourhood again, handing out bags despite his walking stick 😊

grounding: A teenager organises a neighbourhood cleanup and feels needed in a way average marks never gave him.

passage: Why do I coach the under-tens, Sabina? Honestly, it started because my cousin dumped the job on me. I'm a very average midfielder. I've never been picked for district. But on the first evening at the park, a tiny kid called Moinak cried because he kept missing the ball. I showed him to watch the ball, not his feet, and twenty minutes later he scored into the empty goal and ran round the whole park screaming. I was screaming too. Now twelve kids wait for me every Tuesday and Thursday. If I'm late, they phone my mum. At school I'm roll number 23. At the park I'm Karthik anna. That's a different feeling. My marks didn't change. I did.

qa.q: What did Karthik show Moinak?
qa.a: To watch the ball, not his feet.

qa.q: What is Karthik feeling when he says, "My marks didn't change. I did"?
qa.a: He feels a new sense of worth from being needed at the park, something his average marks and roll number never gave him.

qa.q: Which moment was the turning point for Karthik, and why?
qa.a: When Moinak scored after his tip and they both screamed; it showed Karthik he could make a real difference, so he kept coming.

qa.q: How might Moinak have felt when he scored into the empty goal?
qa.a: Moinak probably felt thrilled and proud after crying over missed balls, which is why he ran round the whole park screaming.

grounding: A teenager who coaches younger children finds a sense of worth in being needed that grades and status did not give.

passage:
I'm Anirban, Dolma's cousin, and I live two floors above her in our Darjeeling colony. I can't tell you what goes on inside her, only what I've seen. At school Dolma is middling: average marks, not on any team, the kind of girl teachers forget to name.
Last winter she cleared out the empty garage behind Block C, borrowed a mat and a crate of old picture books, and put up a sign: Saturday Story Corner, ages 4 to 8. By March there were eleven kids. Little Karma now waits at the gate at nine.
I've watched her read the same bear book three times in a row without sighing. She kneels to tie shoelaces and remembers every child's name. When she walks home afterwards, she stands straighter than she does on report-card day.

qa.q: What sign did Dolma put up?
qa.a: Saturday Story Corner, ages 4 to 8.

qa.q: What might Dolma's straighter walk home suggest, even though Anirban can't be sure?
qa.a: It suggests she feels proud and valued, since being needed by the children gives her a sense of worth her average marks don't.

qa.q: What choice turned an empty garage into something meaningful?
qa.a: Dolma chose to clear it out and start the story corner, turning her Saturdays into something useful to others.

qa.q: What might the Story Corner mean to little Karma?
qa.a: It may be the best part of Karma's week, with someone who knows Karma's name and reads patiently.

grounding: A cousin observes a teenager with average marks who starts a story corner for small children and seems to find a sense of worth in being needed.

passage:
Monday. Parveen, fifteen, didn't make the school quiz team, again. That evening she signed up as a helper at the Saturday maths club for the government primary school down the road, mainly to stop thinking about it.
Saturday. She sat on a bench with Ujjwal, nine, who hid his notebook whenever fractions came up. She cut a roti-sized circle of paper into halves, then quarters. On the third try Ujjwal said, "Oh! So a quarter is smaller than a half even though four is bigger!" and looked at her as if she'd done magic.
A month later. Her report card was ordinary. She noticed she didn't mind as much. On Saturday Ujjwal came running, notebook open, to show her a sum with a red tick.

qa.q: What did Parveen cut into halves and then quarters?
qa.a: A roti-sized circle of paper.

qa.q: Why did Parveen mind her ordinary report card less a month later?
qa.a: She felt less disappointed, because being needed by Ujjwal gave her a sense of worth that marks and the quiz team didn't.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Parveen at the maths club?
qa.a: When Ujjwal finally understood quarters and looked at her as if she'd done magic, showing her she was really useful.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel running to show Parveen his red tick?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and eager to share it with the person who helped him understand. 🎉

grounding: After missing the quiz team, a teenager helps younger children with maths and finds a sense of worth in being needed that grades did not give.
